transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-20 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Carlos (Peregrine Lead ML), Priya (Infra), Evan (CTO), Anika (Security)

[00:00:02] Jordan: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. We'll kick off — this is a technical deep dive for Peregrine's long context workload. Maya and Liam are going to drive into runtime behavior and we'll leave time at the end for security and deployment questions.

[00:00:16] Carlos: Thanks Jordan. Quick note, we're trying to get stable inferencing for documents up to ~200k tokens. That's the engineering ask from search + summarization pipelines.

[00:00:29] Maya: Great. To set expectations, 200k is not just a big batch, it's a different class of memory and kernel scheduling problem. We'll cover chunking, sparse attention, and how the KV cache gets sharded across devices.

[00:00:45] Priya: One constraint on our side: our on-prem racks are 4x H100-ish nodes with NVLink disabled for security reasons; PCIe only. So we need patterns that work without full peer access.

[00:01:03] Liam: Okay that matters a lot for KV routing. If NVLink isn't available, the cost of KV scatter/gather goes up and we often prefer local per-shard prefix caching or a hybrid TTL cache.

[00:01:18] [00:01:23] Maya: Quick note on language — I'll use 'chunks' for contiguous window segments, 'stitching' for recombining outputs, and 'KV sharding' when we split key/value caches across GPUs.

[00:01:34] Evan: Curious — what sparse attention variants are you seeing work in prod? We've experimented with block-sparse and top-k global tokens but not at 200k.

[00:01:46] Maya: In our internal benchmarks, a combination of local-window attention + global routing for anchor tokens (think retrieval-augmented tokens and document boundaries) gives best latency/cost tradeoff. Block-sparse helps for encoder-heavy ops but decoder streaming needs careful causal masking.

[00:02:05] Carlos: Can you explain the 'anchor' concept? Is it computed offline or on-the-fly?

[00:02:13] Maya: Good question. Anchors can be precomputed during ingestion (e.g., section headers, retrieval hits) or online via a lightweight tokenizer scorer. The key is to keep the anchor set small per chunk — 64 or 128 anchors per 32k chunk — that way the global attention footprint is O(anchors * chunks) instead of O(total tokens^2).

[00:02:41] [00:02:45] Liam: Also, if you're doing streaming generation across chunks, you can maintain a compressed representation of previous chunks' keys (quantized or PCA compressed) and only reconstruct when higher fidelity is required. That lowers memory but increases CPU deserialization overhead.

[00:02:59] Priya: Are you recommending quantized KV to save memory? We worry about quality regression on summarization tasks.

[00:03:08] Maya: Short answer: yes, with caveats. 4-bit quantization (e.g., GPTQ-style) for the activations in KV caches often works for retrieval+ranking tasks. For extractive summarization quality we recommend hybrid: store recent KVs in full precision and archive older KVs in 4-bit with scale offsets. We saw <1% ROUGE delta in most tests but your mileage may vary.

[00:03:34] Carlos: That hybrid sounds promising. How do you handle mismatch when you reconstruct older KVs?

[00:03:39] Samir (off mic): Usually we apply a per-block dequantization scale and then a short fine-tune or online scaling adjustment if you have reference signals.

[00:03:47] [00:03:55] Maya: Right, and Redwood runtime supports policy-based dequantization thresholding — if a chunk is being actively read for generation we promote it to higher precision in memory for the duration of the generation. Automatic eviction policies are configurable via the console.

[00:04:10] Jordan: Can we show the benchmark graphic? I shared a link earlier to the 200k emulation run. It's on the console (link: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/200k-peregrine).

[00:04:20] Jordan: (screen-share) this is an emulated 200k trace using synthetic chunking and anchor selection. The left pane shows latency P50/P95 and the right shows GPU memory breakdown by KV and model activation.

[00:04:35] Carlos: The P95 in this graph spikes a lot at chunk boundaries — why?

[00:04:40] Maya: Those spikes are from re-sharding and cold reads: when a chunk needs to retrieve keys from a remote shard because NVLink wasn't available in the emulation, there's a network copy plus host-mediated buffer swap. It manifests as a tail latency spike.

[00:04:55] Priya: That's our fear — cold reads will kill the SLA. Any mitigation?

[00:05:00] Liam: A few strategies: prefetching KVs for chunks you predict will be accessed (based on retrieval heuristics), keeping a small in-GPU LRU for hot sections, and using a lightweight approximate cache directory on CPU that indicates whether a full-precision KV exists locally.

[00:05:16] [00:05:25] Maya: Another option is progressive fidelity: serve an initial answer based on compressed KVs and then patch it with a higher-fidelity pass if the user requests more detail. For many UI cases users accept a fast summary then a more detailed second pass.

[00:05:37] Evan: From an ops perspective we need deterministic memory footprints. How do you model GPU memory demand when you have active rehydration?

[00:05:45] Samir: We include a margin in the autoscaler that assumes worst-case active promotion percent (default 10-15%). Redwood's optimizer simulates request mixes to compute effective peak memory and gives configuration knobs — per-request KV budget, per-chunk anchor cap, and eviction thresholds.

[00:06:05] Carlos: Can you talk about kernel selection and the compiler path? We saw strange perf on A100 vs H100 on other stacks.

[00:06:13] Maya: Sure. Redwood compiles model kernels per hardware profile — it selects attention kernels optimized for long sequence lengths; we use tiling + chunked GEMM to keep matmuls in L2/L1 when possible. On H100 some fused kernels are faster, but they require more register pressure. The compiler attempts multiple kernel candidates in a short warm-up and picks the fastest for subsequent batches.

[00:06:37] Priya: Does that mean warm-up runs cost extra time? We can't afford 30s of warm-up per worker.

[00:06:44] Liam: Warm-up is lightweight, usually 1-3 iterations of microbenchmarks at key sequence lengths. You can persist kernel choices to a local artifact so subsequent restarts use cached kernels. We also provide a 'cold-start safe' kernel set for constrained environments.

[00:06:58] [00:07:05] Anika (Security): Quick question on KMS/HSM — if we keep keys on-prem, how does Redwood handle envelope keys and logging? We cannot have private key material leave our VPC.

[00:07:15] Jordan: Good, that's a common enterprise ask. Redwood supports customer-managed KMS via standard envelope encryption. The private key never leaves your HSM; Redwood stores only wrapped keys. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM (we have a Graylog/ELK sample). We'll share the security whitepaper.

[00:07:35] Carlos: Back to runtime: how does batching behave with huge contexts? If each request carries 200k tokens, batch size = 1 seems forced, which kills throughput.

[00:07:48] Maya: Right — you can't batch large contexts naively. Two options: micro-batching within chunked windows (batch together token streams for chunks rather than whole documents) or cross-request streaming batches where requests interleave generation steps so the runtime continuously fills GPU. Continuous batching gives you throughput but increases tail latency slightly; chunked micro-batching reduces memory pressure and keeps latency bounded.

[00:08:12] Priya: Do you have any numbers on token/s throughput with chunked micro-batching?

[00:08:18] Maya: In our emulation with 4xH100-ish configs and chunk size 32k with 128 anchors, we saw an aggregated throughput improvement of ~3.8x vs naive per-doc generation when using chunk-level batching and KV cache reuse. But again, NVLink disabled reduces effective gains by ~20-30% because of remote KV transfer overhead.

[00:08:42] Carlos: About chunk size — why 32k? Could we do 64k chunks and fewer stitches?

[00:08:50] Liam: Larger chunks reduce stitching overhead but increase per-chunk KV memory and the cost of attention kernels. There's a sweet spot that depends on model architecture and your distribution of section lengths. For Peregrine's doc corpus (many medium sections) 16k-32k hits balance memory and compute. We usually recommend doing a knob sweep in your environment.

[00:09:08] [00:09:15] Maya: Also consider variable chunking: let chunk boundaries align with semantic markers (headings, paragraph gaps) instead of fixed-size only — that reduces anchor cross-talk and border effects.

[00:09:26] Carlos: How does Redwood handle consistency when re-sharding KVs across nodes during autoscaling? We can't lose context mid-session.

[00:09:36] Jordan: Redwood's autoscaler prefers scale-out with sticky routing for sessions. We support a migration protocol: when a shard is evicted, a graceful handoff sends a rehydration manifest to the next node and we keep serving from cold storage until the new node fully warms, with a temporary performance penalty but no context loss. You can also pin sessions to a dedicated pool to avoid migration.

[00:09:58] Priya: Pinning would be our preference for production SLAs. Costly but predictable.

[00:10:05] Maya: For predictability we also recommend dedicated capacity pools (Redwood Dedicated) where you control instance types and routing policies. There are also hybrid policies where you use hosted for non-sensitive bursts and private for core traffic.

[00:10:18] [00:10:26] Evan: Any gotchas with quantization + fused kernels? We saw correctness issues with custom fused attention on quantized KVs.

[00:10:34] Maya: Fused kernels assume certain numeric stability; combining them with lower-bit KVs can amplify rounding error. Our runtime will avoid certain fusions if KVs are below a fidelity threshold. You can override but it's not recommended unless you validate on your eval set.

[00:10:50] Carlos: Let's talk eval/quality metrics. We need to correlate latency optimizations to ROUGE/BLEU/dedup metrics.

[00:10:58] Rhea: Redwood has an eval hooks module — you can send prompt sets and references; the platform will run A/B tests across config variants and produce delta reports. We can attach your evals to the perf runs we do for you.

[00:11:12] Priya: For our security folks: does the console artifact export include raw traces? We need to keep PII out of logs.

[00:11:20] Jordan: We can redact traces and provide sanitized traces. The raw traces can remain on your cluster if you're using Redwood Private; we only ingest metrics and anonymized samples. We'll send the security doc that explains retention and redaction.

[00:11:33] [00:11:40] Anika: Please include retention windows and who has access in that doc. Also SAML SSO, RBAC mapping examples.

[00:11:46] Jordan: Will do.

[00:11:50] Carlos: Back to engineering — we want to run the on-prem benchmark. What do you need from us?

[00:11:56] Maya: A test cluster with the same NIC topology as production, example document corpus (or synthetic trace), and a small seed of labeled eval prompts. We'll provide perf scripts, kernel caches, and a reproducible config. Ideally you enable time-synced logging (NTP) and capture nvidia-smi, dmesg, and iostat during runs.

[00:12:18] Priya: We'll stand that up. I already added a ticket in our tracker.

[00:12:22] Liam: One operational tip: If NVLink is disabled, set the KV sharding policy to 'local-first' in the runtime config to minimize remote reads; it's conservative but stable.

[00:12:33] [00:12:40] Maya: Also consider a small on-GPU LRU that keeps ~5% of memory reserved for hot KVs. It's easy to config and can cut tail latencies significantly.

[00:12:51] Carlos: Anything else we should be aware of with 200k+ contexts?

[00:12:55] Maya: Monitoring and synthetic load are key. Watch token-level P99, GPU memcpy rates, and CPU deserialization. We've seen teams miss an expensive CPU-side json parse step that serialized across requests and became the real bottleneck.

[00:13:10] Jordan: Time check — we've got about 10 minutes left. Any legal/procurement notes?

[00:13:15] Evan: We'll need standard enterprise terms and the SLA details for dedicated pools. Also clarify data residency.

[00:13:21] Jordan: We'll send a draft term sheet.

[00:13:25] [00:13:30] Maya: Quick demo note: after the bench run we'll do a capture and annotate hotspots in the trace so you can see exactly which kernels and memcpy ops caused spikes.

[00:13:40] Carlos: Sounds good. One last thing — does Redwood support checkpointed context? Like storing a compact summary state we can resume from?

[00:13:49] Maya: We have a prototype 'context snapshot' that stores a compressed state (PCA + centroid tokens) that lets you warm up a session faster. It's not GA but we can share the prototype and test it in your environment.

[00:14:03] Priya: We'll take it.

[00:14:06] Jordan: Okay wrapping up. I'll summarize next steps.

[00:14:10] Jordan: Action items: Maya will provide kernel selection notes and perf scripts; Priya will provision test cluster; Maya+Liam will run bench with Carlos and share sanitized traces; Jordan will send security whitepaper and term sheet. We'll reconvene after the benchmark.

[00:14:26] Carlos: Thanks everyone. This was useful.

[00:14:29] Jordan: Thanks all. End call.

Post-call notes (auto):
- Recording includes a screen-share with perf graphs (link in CRM).
- Candidate optimizations: local-first KV sharding, chunk-size sweep (16k-32k), hybrid KV quantization, small on-GPU LRU, progressive fidelity for UI flows.
- Risk: NVLink-disabled environments will see 15-30% perf degradation; mitigations enumerated above.
